items.title: Integrations
items.text:
UserHarbor core does not include database or email-provider implementations. Those responsibilities are handled by adapters that implement the core UserStore and EmailSender protocols.

Official integrations:

  • userharbor-sqlalchemy provides a SQLAlchemy-based UserStore
  • userharbor-smtp provides an SMTP-based EmailSender
  • userharbor-fastapi provides FastAPI routes and dependency helpers

See the integrations documentation for detailed setup instructions.

Install the official adapters through the core package extras:

pip install "userharbor[sqlalchemy,smtp,fastapi]"

Or install only the adapter you need:

pip install userharbor-sqlalchemy
pip install userharbor-smtp
pip install userharbor-fastapi

The FastAPI adapter can also be installed through its dedicated core extra:

pip install "userharbor[fastapi]"

items.title: When to use each adapter
items.text:
Use userharbor-sqlalchemy when your application already uses SQLAlchemy or when you want UserHarbor data stored in a relational database.

Use userharbor-smtp when your email provider exposes SMTP credentials and you want a simple email sender without provider-specific SDKs.

Use userharbor-fastapi when your application uses FastAPI and you want ready-to-use account routes, bearer-session authentication, and dependency helpers for current users, roles, and permissions.

All adapters can be replaced with custom implementations as long as they match the core protocols or compose a configured UserHarbor instance.

See Custom integrations for guidance on building your own storage, email, framework, or provider adapter.

items.title: Custom Integrations
items.text:
UserHarbor integrations should live outside the core package. The core library owns account-management rules, token generation, token hashing, and password hashing. Integrations provide infrastructure-specific behavior behind small protocols.

Common integration types include:

  • database or ORM-backed UserStore implementations
  • email-provider EmailSender implementations
  • framework packages that wire UserHarbor into routes, dependencies, or request handling
  • provider adapters for services such as SendGrid, Resend, Mailgun, Redis, or MongoDB

Before creating a new adapter, review the official implementations:

https://github.com/userharbor/userharbor-sqlalchemy
https://github.com/userharbor/userharbor-smtp

items.title: Package structure
items.text:
Keep custom integrations as separate packages. A typical package can be small:

userharbor-myadapter/
    pyproject.toml
    README.md
    src/
        userharbor_myadapter/
            __init__.py
            py.typed
            store.py
            sender.py
    tests/

Only include the files your adapter needs. A storage adapter does not need an email sender, and an email adapter does not need database code.

items.title: UserStore integrations
items.text:
Implement UserStore when your adapter is responsible for persistence.

UserStore is one required contract, but it is composed from smaller protocols for readability:

  • UserAccountStore
  • TokenStore
  • RoleStore
  • PermissionStore

Adapter packages should still pass one store object to UserHarbor.

from contextlib import AbstractContextManager
from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import datetime

from userharbor.interfaces import CreateUserRequest, UserList, UserStore, UserToken


@dataclass
class MyUser:
    username: str
    email: str
    verified: bool


class MyUserStore(UserStore[MyUser]):
    def transaction(self) -> AbstractContextManager[None]:
        ...

    def create_user(self, user: CreateUserRequest) -> None:
        ...

    def set_user_verified(self, username: str) -> None:
        ...

    def delete_user(self, username: str) -> None:
        ...

    def get_user_by_username(self, username: str) -> MyUser | None:
        ...

    def get_user_by_email(self, email: str) -> MyUser | None:
        ...

    def list_users(
        self,
        *,
        limit: int = 50,
        offset: int = 0,
        order: str = "username",
        query: str | None = None,
    ) -> UserList[MyUser]:
        ...

    def get_password_hash(self, username: str) -> str:
        ...

    def set_password_hash(self, username: str, password_hash: str) -> None:
        ...

    # TokenStore

    def get_email_verification(self, token_hash: str) -> UserToken | None:
        ...

    def set_email_verification(self, verification: UserToken) -> None:
        ...

    def remove_email_verification(self, token_hash: str) -> None:
        ...

    def get_session(self, token_hash: str) -> UserToken | None:
        ...

    def add_session(self, session: UserToken) -> None:
        ...

    def remove_session(self, token_hash: str) -> None:
        ...

    def remove_all_sessions(self, username: str) -> None:
        ...

    def refresh_session(self, token_hash: str, new_expires_at: datetime) -> None:
        ...

    def get_password_reset(self, token_hash: str) -> UserToken | None:
        ...

    def set_password_reset(self, reset: UserToken) -> None:
        ...

    def remove_password_reset(self, token_hash: str) -> None:
        ...

    def remove_password_reset_for_user(self, username: str) -> None:
        ...

    # RoleStore

    def create_role(self, role: str) -> None:
        ...

    def delete_role(self, role: str) -> None:
        ...

    def list_roles(self) -> set[str]:
        ...

    def role_exists(self, role: str) -> bool:
        ...

    def grant_role_to_user(self, username: str, role: str) -> None:
        ...

    def revoke_role_from_user(self, username: str, role: str) -> None:
        ...

    def get_user_roles(self, username: str) -> set[str]:
        ...

    # PermissionStore

    def create_permission(self, permission: str) -> None:
        ...

    def delete_permission(self, permission: str) -> None:
        ...

    def list_permissions(self) -> set[str]:
        ...

    def permission_exists(self, permission: str) -> bool:
        ...

    def grant_permission_to_role(self, role: str, permission: str) -> None:
        ...

    def revoke_permission_from_role(self, role: str, permission: str) -> None:
        ...

    def get_role_permissions(self, role: str) -> set[str]:
        ...

    def get_user_permissions(self, username: str) -> set[str]:
        ...

A UserStore is responsible for:

  • creating and deleting users
  • storing password hashes
  • storing email verification token hashes
  • storing session token hashes
  • storing password reset token hashes
  • storing role and permission definitions
  • storing role-to-permission assignments
  • storing user-to-role assignments
  • removing sessions and tokens
  • updating session expiration when sliding session refresh is enabled
  • providing transaction boundaries for multi-step updates

The store should never store raw tokens. UserHarbor passes token hashes to the store and keeps raw token handling in the core flow.

User lookups and list items can return any public user type that provides username, email, and verified. Parameterize UserStore with that concrete type so UserHarbor.get_current_user() and harbor.users preserve it in type checkers. See User Manager for usage examples.

items.title: Contract semantics
items.text:
A conforming UserStore must preserve the behavior expected by UserHarbor, not only provide methods with matching signatures. In particular:

  • usernames are unique using Unicode casefold() comparison while preserving the original casing
  • get_user_by_username() compares usernames using Unicode casefold() and returns the stored user with their original username casing
  • email addresses are unique; UserHarbor normalizes them to lowercase before passing them to the store
  • creating a user and their initial email verification token is atomic
  • a newly created user is not verified
  • setting a new email verification token removes the user's previous verification token
  • setting a new password reset token removes the user's previous reset token
  • changing a user's password removes their active password reset token
  • deleting a user removes their verification tokens, password reset tokens, sessions, and role assignments; reusing the username must not restore the previous account's roles or permissions
  • deleting a missing user, token, session, role, or permission is a no-op
  • refreshing a missing session and marking a missing user as verified are no-ops
  • reading a missing user or token returns None
  • list_users() returns a UserList with public user items and a total counting all matches before pagination, including when the requested page is empty
  • listing searches username or email for the literal query substring without case sensitivity; whitespace around the query is ignored, and an empty query lists all users
  • listing sorts by the named storage field, with an optional - prefix for descending order; username ordering uses casefold(), and equal sort values are ordered by the casefolded username ascending
  • listing applies ordering and filtering before offset and limit; unknown order fields raise an error rather than falling back to a default
  • reading roles or effective permissions for a missing user returns an empty set
  • reading or updating a password hash for a missing user raises KeyError
  • granting or revoking the same relationship more than once is idempotent
  • deleting roles and permissions removes their relationship assignments

The shared contract tests are the executable specification for these rules. Backend-specific exception types and persistence details remain the adapter's responsibility.

items.title: Transactions
items.text:
transaction() should return a context manager. UserHarbor uses it around operations that update multiple related records, such as email verification, password reset, password change, account deletion, and role or permission assignment.

A conforming store must commit when the block finishes successfully and roll back every change from the block when an exception is raised. Nested transaction() calls must participate in the outer transaction.

A nullcontext() can be useful in an early prototype or a deliberately simple test double, but it does not satisfy the complete UserStore contract and will not pass the shared transaction tests.

items.title: Testing
items.text:
Every UserStore integration should run the shared contract tests provided by UserHarbor. Import the complete suite in one test module:

# tests/test_user_store_contract.py

from userharbor.testing.user_store_contract import *  # noqa: F403

Then provide a function-scoped user_store fixture in the integration:

# tests/conftest.py

import pytest


@pytest.fixture
def user_store():
    store = create_user_store()
    try:
        yield store
    finally:
        dispose_user_store(store)

The fixture must provide a clean store for every test and release any database connections or other resources afterwards. The shared suite verifies users, password hashes, paginated user listings, verification and reset tokens, sessions, roles, permissions, assignments, and transaction behavior through the public UserStore interface.

Keep backend-specific tests in the integration repository. Examples include database schema and migration tests, provider-specific errors, custom model mapping, connection handling, and backend-specific transaction behavior.

See UserStore contract tests for instructions on developing contracts and testing them against a local UserHarbor checkout before a new version is published.

items.title: Start from the template
items.text:
userharbor-inmemory is a minimal, contract-tested UserStore implementation and an official GitHub template for building custom storage integrations. It contains a complete in-memory store, package metadata, test and publishing workflows, and the shared contract setup described above.

Select Use this template in the repository or open Create a new repository from the template. The generated project starts with a passing contract suite, so the in-memory implementation can be replaced incrementally while the tests continue to verify the required behavior.

After creating a repository:

  1. Rename the distribution, import package, store class, and project metadata.
  2. Replace the in-memory dictionaries and snapshot transaction with the target backend.
  3. Update the user_store fixture to create a clean backend and dispose of its resources after every test.
  4. Keep the shared contract import and add separate tests for backend-specific schema, errors, mapping, connection, and transaction behavior.

The package can also be installed directly for application tests and examples:

pip install userharbor-inmemory

from userharbor_inmemory import InMemoryUserStore


store = InMemoryUserStore()

Each store instance starts empty and retains data only for its own lifetime. It does not provide persistent storage, cross-process sharing, durable transactions, or concurrency guarantees, so it should not be used as a production database.

items.title: EmailSender integrations
items.text:
Implement EmailSender when your adapter is responsible for message delivery.

from userharbor.interfaces import EmailSender


class MyEmailSender(EmailSender):
    def send_verification(
        self,
        username: str,
        email: str,
        verification_token: str,
    ) -> None:
        ...

    def send_password_reset(
        self,
        username: str,
        email: str,
        reset_token: str,
    ) -> None:
        ...

    def send_email_verified(self, username: str, email: str) -> None:
        ...

    def send_password_changed(self, username: str, email: str) -> None:
        ...

    def send_account_deleted(self, username: str, email: str) -> None:
        ...

An EmailSender should only send messages. It should not decide whether a token is valid, hash tokens, verify users, or reset passwords. Those responsibilities belong to UserHarbor core.

items.title: Testing
items.text:
For EmailSender, cover:

  • verification messages
  • password reset messages
  • email-verified messages
  • password-changed messages
  • account-deleted messages
  • subject and sender configuration
  • template rendering, if templates are supported
  • provider authentication or API calls using fakes

items.title: Framework integrations
items.text:
Framework integrations should compose UserHarbor with framework-specific tools instead of moving domain behavior into the framework package.

A framework adapter may provide:

  • dependency helpers
  • route or router factories
  • request-to-command mapping
  • response models
  • examples for configuring stores and email senders

It should avoid hard-coding one database or email provider unless that is the explicit purpose of the package. Prefer accepting a configured UserHarbor instance or accepting UserStore and EmailSender implementations from the application.

items.title: Public API
items.text:
Export the main adapter class from the package root:

from .store import MyUserStore

__all__ = ["MyUserStore"]

If the package is typed, include py.typed and configure packaging so it is included in distributions.

items.title: Naming
items.text:
Use a clear package name that identifies the target integration:

userharbor-sqlalchemy
userharbor-smtp
userharbor-fastapi
userharbor-sendgrid
userharbor-redis

Keep the adapter focused. If one package starts combining unrelated storage, email, and framework behavior, split it into smaller packages.

items.title: FastAPI Integration
items.text:
userharbor-fastapi provides a FastAPI adapter for UserHarbor. It exposes account-management routes and dependency helpers while keeping user storage, email delivery, password hashing, token generation, and account rules in UserHarbor core and the configured integrations.

Repository:

https://github.com/userharbor/userharbor-fastapi

items.title: Installation
items.text:
pip install userharbor-fastapi

You can also install it through the core package extra:

pip install "userharbor[fastapi]"

Or install all official adapters together:

pip install "userharbor[all]"

The package depends on userharbor and FastAPI.

Install storage and email adapters separately. For example:

pip install userharbor-sqlalchemy
pip install userharbor-smtp

items.title: What it provides
items.text:
The adapter provides:

  • a FastAPI APIRouter
  • account routes for registration, email verification, login, logout, password reset, password change, and account deletion
  • bearer session token authentication
  • current-user and optional-user dependencies
  • role and permission dependencies
  • UserHarbor exception to HTTP error mapping
  • configurable user serialization for route responses

It does not provide a database implementation or email delivery implementation. Pass a configured UserHarbor instance that already has a UserStore and EmailSender.

items.title: Basic usage
items.text:
from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI
from userharbor import UserHarbor
from userharbor_fastapi import UserHarborFastAPI


harbor = UserHarbor(
    secret_key="your-secret-key",
    store=store,
    email_sender=email_sender,
)

auth = UserHarborFastAPI(harbor)

app = FastAPI()
app.include_router(auth.router, prefix="/auth", tags=["auth"])


@app.get("/me")
def me(user=Depends(auth.current_user)):
    return user


@app.get("/admin")
def admin(user=Depends(auth.require_role("admin"))):
    return user


@app.get("/billing")
def billing(user=Depends(auth.require_permission("billing.read"))):
    return user

items.title: Built-in routes
items.text:
The adapter exposes these routes through auth.router:

POST   /register
POST   /verify-email
POST   /resend-verification
POST   /login
POST   /logout
POST   /logout-all
GET    /me
POST   /password-reset/request
POST   /password-reset/confirm
POST   /password/change
DELETE /account

Mount the router under the prefix used by your application:

app.include_router(auth.router, prefix="/auth", tags=["auth"])

With that prefix, the login route is available at /auth/login, the current user route at /auth/me, and so on.

The routes are also visible in FastAPI's generated Swagger UI:

items.title: Authentication
items.text:
POST /login returns a bearer-compatible response:

{
  "access_token": "session-token",
  "token_type": "bearer"
}

Send the session token on protected requests:

Authorization: Bearer <session-token>

The token is the UserHarbor session token returned by harbor.login().

items.title: Dependencies
items.text:
Use auth.current_user when a route requires a valid session:

@app.get("/account")
def account(user=Depends(auth.current_user)):
    return user

Use auth.optional_user when authentication should be optional:

@app.get("/homepage")
def homepage(user=Depends(auth.optional_user)):
    return {"authenticated": user is not None}

Use role and permission dependencies for authorization:

@app.get("/admin")
def admin(user=Depends(auth.require_role("admin"))):
    return user


@app.get("/invoices")
def invoices(user=Depends(auth.require_permission("billing.invoices.read"))):
    return user

auth.require_role() and auth.require_permission() return the current user when authorization succeeds. They map invalid or expired sessions to authentication errors and missing roles or permissions to authorization errors.

items.title: User serialization
items.text:
By default, /me returns the public UserHarbor user fields:

{
  "username": "jane",
  "email": "jane@example.com",
  "verified": true
}

Pass user_serializer when your application returns a richer user object from its store and wants to expose a custom public response shape:

auth = UserHarborFastAPI(
    harbor,
    user_serializer=lambda user: {
        "username": user.username,
        "email": user.email,
        "verified": user.verified,
        "display_name": user.display_name,
    },
)

The serializer is used by the built-in /me route.

items.title: Error responses
items.text:
UserHarbor exceptions are converted into structured FastAPI errors:

{
  "detail": {
    "detail": "Invalid username or password",
    "code": "invalid_credentials"
  }
}

The adapter maps common failures as follows:

  • invalid credentials and invalid sessions return 401 Unauthorized
  • valid sessions without the required role or permission return 403 Forbidden
  • unknown roles and permissions return 404 Not Found
  • invalid input and invalid verification or password reset tokens return 400 Bad Request
  • username conflicts return 409 Conflict

items.title: Combining official adapters
items.text:
A typical FastAPI application can combine the official SQLAlchemy, SMTP, and FastAPI integrations:

import os

from fastapi import FastAPI
from sqlalchemy import create_engine
from sqlalchemy.orm import sessionmaker
from userharbor import UserHarbor
from userharbor_fastapi import UserHarborFastAPI
from userharbor_smtp import SMTPEmailSender
from userharbor_sqlalchemy import SQLAlchemyUserStore


engine = create_engine("sqlite:///users.db")
SessionLocal = sessionmaker(bind=engine)

store = SQLAlchemyUserStore(SessionLocal)
store.metadata.create_all(engine)

email_sender = SMTPEmailSender(
    host=os.getenv("HOST", "smtp.example.com"),
    port=int(os.getenv("PORT", 587)),
    username=os.getenv("USERNAME"),
    password=os.getenv("PASSWORD"),
    from_email=os.getenv("USERNAME", ""),
)

harbor = UserHarbor(
    secret_key="your-secret-key",
    store=store,
    email_sender=email_sender,
)

auth = UserHarborFastAPI(harbor)

app = FastAPI()
app.include_router(auth.router, prefix="/auth", tags=["auth"])


if __name__ == "__main__":
    import uvicorn

    uvicorn.run(app, host="0.0.0.0", port=8000)

In production applications, use your normal configuration system for secrets, SMTP credentials, and database URLs.

items.title: SMTP Integration
items.text:
userharbor-smtp provides SMTPEmailSender, an EmailSender implementation that sends verification, password-reset, and account security notification messages through SMTP.

Repository:

https://github.com/userharbor/userharbor-smtp

items.title: Installation
items.text:
pip install userharbor-smtp

You can also install it through the core package extra:

pip install "userharbor[smtp]"

items.title: Basic usage
items.text:
from userharbor_smtp import SMTPEmailSender

email_sender = SMTPEmailSender(
    host="smtp.example.com",
    port=587,
    username="smtp-user",
    password="smtp-password",
    from_email="noreply@example.com",
    from_name="UserHarbor",
)

Pass the sender to UserHarbor as its email_sender. UserHarbor calls it when it needs to send:

  • email verification messages
  • password reset messages
  • email-verified notifications
  • password-changed notifications
  • account-deleted notifications

items.title: Configuration
items.text:
SMTPEmailSender(
    host="smtp.example.com",
    from_email="noreply@example.com",
    port=587,
    username=None,
    password=None,
    from_name=None,
    template_dir=None,
    template_context=None,
    verification_subject="Verify your email",
    password_reset_subject="Reset your password",
    email_verified_subject="Email verified",
    password_changed_subject="Password changed",
    account_deleted_subject="Account deleted",
    use_starttls=True,
    use_ssl=False,
    ssl_context=None,
    allow_insecure=False,
    timeout=10,
)

Use use_starttls=True for the common SMTP submission flow on port 587. Use use_ssl=True for implicit TLS, commonly on port 465. When use_ssl=True, STARTTLS is not started separately.

The sender uses Python's secure default SSL context, which verifies the SMTP server certificate and hostname. Pass ssl_context only when the application needs a custom trusted certificate authority or TLS policy. At least one of use_starttls and use_ssl must be enabled. Set allow_insecure=True only for a trusted local SMTP relay where plaintext transport is an explicit, deliberate choice.

If both username and password are provided, the sender authenticates before sending the message.

items.title: Templates
items.text:
By default, the package uses bundled HTML templates:

  • verification.html
  • password_reset.html
  • email_verified.html
  • password_changed.html
  • account_deleted.html

To use custom templates, pass a pathlib.Path to a directory containing files with the same names:

from pathlib import Path

email_sender = SMTPEmailSender(
    host="smtp.example.com",
    port=587,
    username="smtp-user",
    password="smtp-password",
    from_email="noreply@example.com",
    template_dir=Path("templates/emails"),
    template_context={"app_url": "https://example.com"},
)

Each template receives:

  • username
  • email

Verification and password reset templates also receive token.

Use template_context to add variables to every template. Built-in variables username, email, and token take precedence over custom values.

Example templates/emails/verification.html:

<p>Hello {{ username }},</p>
<p><a href="{{ app_url }}/auth/verify_email?token={{ token | urlencode }}">Verify {{ email }}</a></p>

Example templates/emails/password_reset.html:

<p>Hello {{ username }},</p>
<p>Use this token to reset your password:</p>
<p><strong>{{ token }}</strong></p>

Example templates/emails/password_changed.html:

<p>Hello {{ username }},</p>
<p>The password for {{ email }} was changed.</p>

items.title: SQLAlchemy Integration
items.text:
userharbor-sqlalchemy provides SQLAlchemyUserStore, a UserStore implementation backed by SQLAlchemy 2.x.

Repository:

https://github.com/userharbor/userharbor-sqlalchemy

items.title: Installation
items.text:
pip install userharbor-sqlalchemy

This package depends on userharbor and SQLAlchemy 2.x.

You can also install it through the core package extra:

pip install "userharbor[sqlalchemy]"

items.title: What it stores
items.text:
The adapter persists:

  • users
  • password hashes
  • email verification tokens
  • sessions
  • password reset tokens
  • roles
  • permissions
  • user-to-role assignments
  • role-to-permission assignments

Each user has at most one active email verification token and one active password reset token. Storing a new token of either kind removes that user's previous token. Users can have multiple active sessions.

Changing a user's password also removes their active password reset token.

It also updates session expiration when UserHarbor refreshes an active session.

Deleting a user through the store removes their tokens, sessions, and role assignments in the same transaction. This also works with custom user models and SQLite connections without foreign key enforcement. Role and permission definitions, and other users' assignments, are preserved.

It does not send emails, expose HTTP endpoints, or implement application-specific authentication flows.

items.title: Basic usage
items.text:
from sqlalchemy import create_engine
from sqlalchemy.orm import sessionmaker
from userharbor_sqlalchemy import SQLAlchemyUserStore


engine = create_engine("sqlite:///users.db")
SessionLocal = sessionmaker(bind=engine)

store = SQLAlchemyUserStore(SessionLocal)
store.metadata.create_all(engine)

Pass store to UserHarbor as its UserStore implementation.

items.title: Creating tables
items.text:
The adapter exposes SQLAlchemy metadata through the store:

store = SQLAlchemyUserStore(SessionLocal)

store.metadata.create_all(engine)

The built-in table names are:

  • userharbor_users
  • userharbor_email_verifications
  • userharbor_sessions
  • userharbor_password_resets
  • userharbor_roles
  • userharbor_permissions
  • userharbor_user_roles
  • userharbor_role_permissions

In applications that use migrations, include these models in your migration metadata instead of calling create_all() at runtime.

items.title: Alembic migrations
items.text:
Applications that use Alembic should let migrations own schema creation. Do not call store.metadata.create_all(engine) during application startup after Alembic has been configured.

Install and initialize Alembic if the application does not already use it:

pip install alembic
alembic init migrations

items.title: Keep the store definition separate
items.text:
Define the SQLAlchemy store in a small module that only depends on the database configuration:

# app/user_store.py
from app.database import SessionLocal
from userharbor_sqlalchemy import SQLAlchemyUserStore


user_store = SQLAlchemyUserStore(SessionLocal)

Import this store from both the application setup and Alembic. Avoid importing the fully configured UserHarbor service from migrations/env.py: constructing that service may require unrelated secrets, SMTP settings, or framework setup, while Alembic only needs the store metadata.

items.title: Configure target metadata
items.text:
When the application uses its own declarative base and the built-in UserHarbor user model, the application and UserHarbor have separate MetaData objects. Alembic accepts a sequence of metadata collections for autogeneration:

# migrations/env.py
# Import application models so they register with Base.metadata.
from app import models as _models
from app.database import Base
from app.user_store import user_store


target_metadata = [Base.metadata, user_store.metadata]

Keep the generated target_metadata=target_metadata argument in both calls to context.configure(). Import every application model module before assigning target_metadata; otherwise Alembic cannot detect those tables.

If UserHarbor owns all SQLAlchemy models in the application, a single metadata collection is enough:

target_metadata = user_store.metadata

Alembic requires table keys to be unique across a sequence of metadata collections. See its documentation for autogenerating multiple metadata collections.

items.title: When using a custom user model
items.text:
When user_model is provided, the adapter reuses that model's metadata for all generated UserHarbor tables:

# app/user_store.py
from app.database import SessionLocal
from app.models import AppUser
from userharbor_sqlalchemy import SQLAlchemyUserStore


user_store = SQLAlchemyUserStore(
    SessionLocal,
    user_model=AppUser,
)

In that case, use the shared metadata once instead of passing the same metadata twice:

# migrations/env.py
from app import models as _models
from app.user_store import user_store


target_metadata = user_store.metadata

See Custom user model for the fields required by AppUser.

items.title: Generate and apply the migration
items.text:
After configuring target_metadata, generate the migration:

alembic revision --autogenerate -m "create UserHarbor tables"

Review the generated migration before applying it. It should create the UserHarbor tables listed above along with any pending application schema changes. Then apply it and verify that the database matches the metadata:

alembic upgrade head
alembic check

Future adapter model changes can be handled through the same autogenerate, review, and upgrade workflow.

items.title: Custom user model
items.text:
By default, the adapter creates and uses its own userharbor_users table. If your application already owns a user table, pass that SQLAlchemy model as user_model:

from sqlalchemy import Boolean, String, create_engine
from sqlalchemy.orm import DeclarativeBase, Mapped, mapped_column, sessionmaker
from userharbor_sqlalchemy import SQLAlchemyUserStore


class AppBase(DeclarativeBase):
    pass


class AppUser(AppBase):
    __tablename__ = "app_users"

    username: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(String(255), primary_key=True)
    username_key: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(String(255), unique=True, index=True)
    email: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(String(320), unique=True, index=True)
    password_hash: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(String(512))
    verified: Mapped[bool] = mapped_column(Boolean, default=False)
    display_name: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(String(255), default="Anonymous")


engine = create_engine("sqlite:///users.db")
SessionLocal = sessionmaker(bind=engine)

store = SQLAlchemyUserStore(
    SessionLocal,
    user_model=AppUser,
)
store.metadata.create_all(engine)

Custom user models must provide:

  • username
  • username_key
  • email
  • password_hash
  • verified

SQLAlchemyUserStore writes username.casefold() to username_key. The column must be unique so username lookup and uniqueness remain case-insensitive while username preserves its original casing.

The token and role assignment tables are still created by the adapter. Their user foreign keys point to the table configured through user_model. When a custom user model is provided, the adapter reuses that model's metadata, so store.metadata contains both the application user model and the generated UserHarbor token, role, permission, and assignment models.

items.title: Custom user mapping
items.text:
By default, SQLAlchemy user rows are mapped to a small public user object with username, email, and verified. Pass user_mapper when your application wants to return a richer public user type:

from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass
class AppPublicUser:
    username: str
    email: str
    verified: bool
    display_name: str


store = SQLAlchemyUserStore(
    SessionLocal,
    user_model=AppUser,
    user_mapper=lambda user: AppPublicUser(
        username=user.username,
        email=user.email,
        verified=user.verified,
        display_name=user.display_name,
    ),
)

user_mapper is used by get_user_by_username(), get_user_by_email(), and every item returned by list_users(). Token methods continue to return UserToken values.

items.title: Roles and permissions
items.text:
SQLAlchemyUserStore implements the complete role and permission persistence contract required by UserHarbor:

harbor.roles.create("admin")
harbor.permissions.create("users.delete")
harbor.roles.grant_permission("admin", "users.delete")
harbor.grant_role("jane", "admin")

Roles and permissions are stored separately from users. User permissions are derived through the userharbor_user_roles and userharbor_role_permissions tables.

Deleting a role removes that role from users and removes its permission assignments. Deleting a permission removes it from every role.

items.title: Sessions and transactions
items.text:
SQLAlchemyUserStore receives a session factory:

store = SQLAlchemyUserStore(SessionLocal)

Each store method opens a session when no UserHarbor transaction is active. SQLAlchemyUserStore.transaction() is used by UserHarbor for multi-step operations such as email verification, password reset, password change, account deletion, and other flows that need related writes to commit or roll back together.

Role and permission methods use the same session handling as the account and token methods.

Successful transaction blocks are committed. Exceptions roll back changes from the block.

Session refreshes are persisted by the store when UserHarbor's sliding session expiration is enabled.

items.title: Tutorials
items.text:
These tutorials show how to build complete application flows with UserHarbor. They are written as practical walkthroughs and explain where UserHarbor ends and where your application or framework code begins.

Start here:

  • FastAPI Authentication with UserHarbor - Build a complete FastAPI application with UserHarbor authentication.
  • FastHTML Application with UserHarbor - Build a complete hypermedia-driven application with a ready-to-use starter.

items.title: FastAPI Authentication with UserHarbor
items.text:
Note

For most FastAPI applications, prefer the ready-made userharbor-fastapi adapter. It provides the router, dependencies, schemas, and HTTP error mapping shown in this tutorial.

This tutorial builds the same ideas step by step.

You will create a small FastAPI application that uses UserHarbor directly for:

  • user registration
  • email verification
  • login
  • bearer session authentication
  • current-user dependencies
  • password reset
  • password change
  • account deletion
  • logout
  • role and permission checks

The goal is to show how the pieces fit together. UserHarbor owns the account rules, password hashing, token generation, token hashing, session validation, and role checks. FastAPI owns HTTP routing, request parsing, response models, and dependency injection.

items.title: Install dependencies
items.text:
Create a virtual environment, then install FastAPI, UserHarbor, and a storage adapter:

pip install "fastapi[standard]"
pip install userharbor
pip install userharbor-sqlalchemy

This tutorial uses the SQLAlchemy store and a small console email sender. In a real application, use your normal database configuration and an email sender such as userharbor-smtp.

items.title: Create main.py
items.text:
Start with the imports and application setup:

from typing import Any

from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI, HTTPException, status
from fastapi.security import HTTPAuthorizationCredentials, HTTPBearer
from pydantic import BaseModel
from sqlalchemy import create_engine
from sqlalchemy.orm import sessionmaker
from userharbor import UserHarbor
from userharbor.exceptions import (
    InvalidCredentialsError,
    InvalidEmailError,
    InvalidPasswordResetTokenError,
    InvalidPermissionError,
    InvalidRoleError,
    InvalidSessionTokenError,
    InvalidUsernameError,
    InvalidVerificationTokenError,
    PermissionDeniedError,
    UnknownPermissionError,
    UnknownRoleError,
    UnverifiedUserError,
    UserHarborError,
    WeakPasswordError,
)
from userharbor_sqlalchemy import SQLAlchemyUserStore


app = FastAPI()
bearer = HTTPBearer(auto_error=False)

HTTPBearer(auto_error=False) lets your code decide exactly how to turn missing or invalid credentials into HTTP responses.

items.title: Add an email sender
items.text:
UserHarbor calls an EmailSender when it needs to send verification tokens, password reset tokens, and account notifications.

For the tutorial, print those messages to the terminal:

class ConsoleEmailSender:
    def send_verification(
        self,
        username: str,
        email: str,
        verification_token: str,
    ) -> None:
        print(f"Verify {username} at {email}: {verification_token}")

    def send_password_reset(
        self,
        username: str,
        email: str,
        reset_token: str,
    ) -> None:
        print(f"Reset password for {username} at {email}: {reset_token}")

    def send_email_verified(self, username: str, email: str) -> None:
        print(f"Email verified for {username} at {email}")

    def send_password_changed(self, username: str, email: str) -> None:
        print(f"Password changed for {username} at {email}")

    def send_account_deleted(self, username: str, email: str) -> None:
        print(f"Account deleted for {username} at {email}")

In production, replace this with an implementation that sends real email.

items.title: Configure UserHarbor
items.text:
Create the SQLAlchemy store, create the tables, and pass the store and email sender to UserHarbor:

engine = create_engine("sqlite:///users.db")
SessionLocal = sessionmaker(bind=engine)

store = SQLAlchemyUserStore(SessionLocal)
store.metadata.create_all(engine)

harbor = UserHarbor(
    secret_key="change-this-secret-key",
    store=store,
    email_sender=ConsoleEmailSender(),
)

The FastAPI application never handles password hashing or token hashing. UserHarbor does that before data reaches the store.

items.title: Define request and response models
items.text:
Use Pydantic models for the HTTP layer:

class RegisterRequest(BaseModel):
    username: str
    email: str
    password: str


class LoginRequest(BaseModel):
    username: str
    password: str


class VerifyEmailRequest(BaseModel):
    token: str


class PasswordResetRequest(BaseModel):
    email: str


class PasswordResetConfirmRequest(BaseModel):
    token: str
    new_password: str


class ChangePasswordRequest(BaseModel):
    old_password: str
    new_password: str


class DeleteAccountRequest(BaseModel):
    password: str


class TokenResponse(BaseModel):
    access_token: str
    token_type: str = "bearer"


class PublicUser(BaseModel):
    username: str
    email: str
    verified: bool

These models are not part of UserHarbor. They are your HTTP contract.

items.title: Map UserHarbor errors to HTTP errors
items.text:
UserHarbor raises domain exceptions. Your web layer should translate them into HTTP responses:

ERROR_CODES: dict[type[UserHarborError], str] = {
    InvalidCredentialsError: "invalid_credentials",
    InvalidEmailError: "invalid_email",
    InvalidPasswordResetTokenError: "invalid_password_reset_token",
    InvalidPermissionError: "invalid_permission",
    InvalidRoleError: "invalid_role",
    InvalidSessionTokenError: "invalid_session_token",
    InvalidUsernameError: "invalid_username",
    InvalidVerificationTokenError: "invalid_verification_token",
    PermissionDeniedError: "permission_denied",
    UnknownPermissionError: "unknown_permission",
    UnknownRoleError: "unknown_role",
    UnverifiedUserError: "unverified_user",
    WeakPasswordError: "weak_password",
}


def error_code(error: UserHarborError) -> str:
    for error_type, code in ERROR_CODES.items():
        if isinstance(error, error_type):
            return code
    return "userharbor_error"


def status_code(error: UserHarborError) -> int:
    if isinstance(error, (InvalidCredentialsError, InvalidSessionTokenError)):
        return status.HTTP_401_UNAUTHORIZED
    if isinstance(error, (PermissionDeniedError, UnverifiedUserError)):
        return status.HTTP_403_FORBIDDEN
    if isinstance(error, (UnknownPermissionError, UnknownRoleError)):
        return status.HTTP_404_NOT_FOUND
    if isinstance(error, InvalidUsernameError) and "already exists" in str(error):
        return status.HTTP_409_CONFLICT
    return status.HTTP_400_BAD_REQUEST


def to_http_error(error: UserHarborError) -> HTTPException:
    return HTTPException(
        status_code=status_code(error),
        detail={
            "detail": str(error) or error.__class__.__name__,
            "code": error_code(error),
        },
        headers={"WWW-Authenticate": "Bearer"}
        if isinstance(error, InvalidSessionTokenError)
        else None,
    )

This keeps authentication failures, authorization failures, and validation errors distinct.

items.title: Register users
items.text:
The registration endpoint parses JSON, calls harbor.register(), and returns a neutral response:

@app.post("/auth/register", status_code=status.HTTP_201_CREATED)
def register(request: RegisterRequest) -> dict[str, str]:
    try:
        harbor.register(
            username=request.username,
            email=request.email,
            password=request.password,
        )
    except UserHarborError as error:
        raise to_http_error(error) from error
    return {"detail": "User registered"}

UserHarbor validates the username, email, and password. It creates the user, stores only the password hash, stores only the verification token hash, and calls the email sender with the raw verification token.

items.title: Verify email addresses
items.text:
Copy the verification token printed by ConsoleEmailSender and send it to this endpoint:

@app.post("/auth/verify-email")
def verify_email(request: VerifyEmailRequest) -> dict[str, str]:
    try:
        harbor.verify_email(request.token)
    except UserHarborError as error:
        raise to_http_error(error) from error
    return {"detail": "Email verified"}

After verification, the user can log in.

items.title: Login and return a bearer token
items.text:
Call harbor.login() and return the session token in a bearer-compatible response:

@app.post("/auth/login", response_model=TokenResponse)
def login(request: LoginRequest) -> TokenResponse:
    try:
        session_token = harbor.login(request.username, request.password)
    except UserHarborError as error:
        raise to_http_error(error) from error
    return TokenResponse(access_token=session_token)

The raw session token is returned to the client once. UserHarbor stores a hash of it through the configured store.

Clients should send the token on later requests:

Authorization: Bearer <session-token>

items.title: Create current-user dependencies
items.text:
Now create the dependency that reads the bearer token and asks UserHarbor for the current user:

def get_session_token(
    credentials: HTTPAuthorizationCredentials | None = Depends(bearer),
) -> str:
    if credentials is None:
        raise HTTPException(
            status_code=status.HTTP_401_UNAUTHORIZED,
            detail="Missing bearer token",
            headers={"WWW-Authenticate": "Bearer"},
        )
    return credentials.credentials


def get_current_user(token: str = Depends(get_session_token)) -> Any:
    try:
        return harbor.get_current_user(token)
    except UserHarborError as error:
        raise to_http_error(error) from error

This is the main connection between FastAPI security dependencies and UserHarbor session validation.

items.title: Protect a route
items.text:
Use Depends(get_current_user) in any route that requires authentication:

def serialize_user(user: Any) -> PublicUser:
    return PublicUser(
        username=user.username,
        email=user.email,
        verified=user.verified,
    )


@app.get("/auth/me", response_model=PublicUser)
def me(user: Any = Depends(get_current_user)) -> PublicUser:
    return serialize_user(user)

If the token is missing, invalid, expired, or points to a deleted user, UserHarbor rejects it.

items.title: Logout
items.text:
Logout removes the current session token:

@app.post("/auth/logout")
def logout(token: str = Depends(get_session_token)) -> dict[str, str]:
    try:
        harbor.logout(token)
    except UserHarborError as error:
        raise to_http_error(error) from error
    return {"detail": "Logged out"}

To remove all sessions for the current user:

@app.post("/auth/logout-all")
def logout_all(token: str = Depends(get_session_token)) -> dict[str, str]:
    try:
        harbor.logout_all(token)
    except UserHarborError as error:
        raise to_http_error(error) from error
    return {"detail": "Logged out from all sessions"}

items.title: Password reset
items.text:
Password reset is split into two routes. The first route sends a reset token if the email belongs to a user:

@app.post("/auth/password-reset/request")
def request_password_reset(request: PasswordResetRequest) -> dict[str, str]:
    try:
        harbor.send_password_reset(request.email)
    except UserHarborError as error:
        raise to_http_error(error) from error
    return {"detail": "Password reset email sent"}

UserHarbor returns neutrally for unknown email addresses, helping reduce email enumeration.

The second route accepts the reset token and the new password:

@app.post("/auth/password-reset/confirm")
def confirm_password_reset(request: PasswordResetConfirmRequest) -> dict[str, str]:
    try:
        harbor.reset_password(
            new_password=request.new_password,
            reset_token=request.token,
        )
    except UserHarborError as error:
        raise to_http_error(error) from error
    return {"detail": "Password reset"}

After a successful reset, UserHarbor removes all sessions for that user.

items.title: Password change
items.text:
Password change requires an existing session and the current password:

@app.post("/auth/password/change")
def change_password(
    request: ChangePasswordRequest,
    token: str = Depends(get_session_token),
) -> dict[str, str]:
    try:
        harbor.change_password(
            old_password=request.old_password,
            new_password=request.new_password,
            session_token=token,
        )
    except UserHarborError as error:
        raise to_http_error(error) from error
    return {"detail": "Password changed"}

UserHarbor invalidates all sessions after a successful password change.

items.title: Delete accounts
items.text:
Account deletion should require both a valid session and the current password:

@app.delete("/auth/account")
def delete_account(
    request: DeleteAccountRequest,
    token: str = Depends(get_session_token),
) -> dict[str, str]:
    try:
        harbor.delete_account(
            password=request.password,
            session_token=token,
        )
    except UserHarborError as error:
        raise to_http_error(error) from error
    return {"detail": "Account deleted"}

UserHarbor removes all sessions before deleting the user and then calls the email sender with an account-deleted notification.

items.title: Add role and permission dependencies
items.text:
Create a dependency factory for permissions:

def require_permission(permission: str):
    def dependency(token: str = Depends(get_session_token)) -> Any:
        try:
            return harbor.require_permission(token, permission)
        except UserHarborError as error:
            raise to_http_error(error) from error

    return dependency

Use it on protected routes:

@app.get("/admin/users")
def list_users(
    user: Any = Depends(require_permission("users.read")),
) -> dict[str, str]:
    return {"detail": f"{user.username} can read users"}

Before this can succeed, the permission and role must exist and the user must have the role:

harbor.roles.create("admin")
harbor.permissions.create("users.read")
harbor.roles.grant_permission("admin", "users.read")
harbor.grant_role("jane", "admin")

In a real application, put that setup in migrations, admin commands, or an internal admin interface.

items.title: Production hardening checklist
items.text:
This tutorial keeps everything in one file so the flow is easy to inspect. For a real application:

  • load secret_key, database URLs, and SMTP credentials from environment variables or a secret manager
  • use a long random secret_key and rotate it carefully, because it is used for token hashing
  • serve the API only over HTTPS
  • replace ConsoleEmailSender with a real email sender
  • use migrations instead of store.metadata.create_all(engine) at runtime
  • decide where roles and permissions are created, such as migrations or admin commands
  • keep bearer tokens out of logs
  • configure CORS explicitly if a browser frontend calls the API
  • add rate limiting around login, password reset, and verification resend
  • return neutral responses for account discovery-sensitive flows
  • write tests for successful flows and for each mapped error response

items.title: Run the app
items.text:
Run the application:

fastapi dev main.py

Open the interactive docs:

http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs

Then try this flow:

  1. Call POST /auth/register
  2. Copy the verification token printed in the terminal
  3. Call POST /auth/verify-email
  4. Call POST /auth/login
  5. Copy the returned access_token
  6. Send it as Authorization: Bearer <token>
  7. Call GET /auth/me

items.title: What you built
items.text:
You now have a FastAPI application that uses UserHarbor directly.

FastAPI handles:

  • routing
  • request parsing
  • response models
  • OpenAPI documentation
  • dependency injection
  • HTTP status codes

UserHarbor handles:

  • account validation
  • password hashing
  • token generation
  • token hashing before storage
  • email verification
  • session validation
  • password reset and password change flows
  • role and permission checks

This is the same boundary used by the userharbor-fastapi adapter. The adapter simply packages this wiring so applications do not have to repeat it.

items.title: FastHTML Application with UserHarbor
items.text: This tutorial builds a Hypermedia-Driven Application (HDA) with FastHTML, HTMX, and UserHarbor. The server returns HTML, and the browser updates the page through HTMX attributes.

items.title: What you will build
items.text:
You will create an application with registration, email verification, login, password recovery, a paginated user list, user details, password changes, and account deletion. Only the account owner sees their password and deletion forms. Basecoat provides the UI components.

Watch the presentation.

Start with the finished application

Use FastHTML Starter as a repository template if you want to run the finished application immediately. Its README contains the setup instructions. This walkthrough explains how to build the same account flows, with a smaller dashboard layout.

FastHTML handles routing, form parsing, and HTML rendering. HTMX sends requests and swaps HTML. UserHarbor handles account validation, password hashing, tokens, sessions, and account operations. Your application decides who may access each page.

items.title: Install dependencies
items.text:
Use Python 3.14 or later, matching the starter, and uv:

uv init --python 3.14 fasthtml-app
cd fasthtml-app
uv add python-fasthtml "userharbor[sqlalchemy,smtp]" \
  fasthtml-basecoatui "fasthtml-tailwindcss[dev]" \
  fasthtml-lucide

The Python wrappers fasthtml-basecoatui, fasthtml-tailwindcss, and fasthtml-lucide provide UI components, stylesheet generation, and icons. No separate JavaScript application or JSON API is needed for these flows.

items.title: Organize the application
items.text:
Use the same separation as the starter:

app/
├── core/             # Settings, UserHarbor instance, shared types
├── components/       # Forms, cards, table, pagination, alerts
│   └── auth/
├── layouts/          # HTML document and page shells
├── pages/            # Components composed into complete pages
├── routes/           # Request parsing and domain calls
├── email_templates/  # Verification and recovery links
├── static/
└── main.py           # Session middleware and mounted applications

Create the directories and package files:

mkdir -p app/core app/components/auth app/layouts app/pages app/routes \
  app/email_templates app/static
touch app/__init__.py app/core/__init__.py app/components/__init__.py \
  app/components/auth/__init__.py app/layouts/__init__.py \
  app/pages/__init__.py app/routes/__init__.py

Save each code block in the file named above it. When a step says to append code, keep the preceding contents of that file. Finish creating the files before starting the application: routes import pages, and pages import their components.

items.title: Configure settings and UserHarbor
items.text:
Create .env at the project root. Choose a random secret key and fill in your SMTP credentials. APP_URL is the public base URL used in email links.

.env
SECRET_KEY=replace-with-a-long-random-secret
SMTP_HOST=smtp.example.com
SMTP_PORT=587
SMTP_USERNAME=your-smtp-username
SMTP_PASSWORD=your-smtp-password
SMTP_FROM_EMAIL=noreply@example.com
APP_URL=http://localhost:8000

Keep .env out of version control. The run command at the end loads it into the process environment. Read those settings in app/core/settings.py:

app/core/settings.py
import os

SECRET_KEY = os.environ["SECRET_KEY"]
SMTP_HOST = os.environ["SMTP_HOST"]
SMTP_PORT = int(os.getenv("SMTP_PORT", "587"))
SMTP_USERNAME = os.getenv("SMTP_USERNAME")
SMTP_PASSWORD = os.getenv("SMTP_PASSWORD")
SMTP_FROM_EMAIL = os.environ["SMTP_FROM_EMAIL"]
APP_URL = os.getenv("APP_URL", "http://localhost:8000")

Configure one shared UserHarbor instance. The SQLAlchemy adapter persists accounts and sessions, and the SMTP adapter sends account emails.

The SQLite URL is relative to the working directory, so running from app/ creates app/users.db. create_all() creates the tables on the first run.

app/core/harbor.py
from pathlib import Path

from sqlalchemy import create_engine
from sqlalchemy.orm import sessionmaker
from userharbor import UserHarbor
from userharbor_smtp import SMTPEmailSender
from userharbor_sqlalchemy import SQLAlchemyUserStore

from .settings import (
    APP_URL,
    SECRET_KEY,
    SMTP_FROM_EMAIL,
    SMTP_HOST,
    SMTP_PASSWORD,
    SMTP_PORT,
    SMTP_USERNAME,
)

engine = create_engine("sqlite:///users.db")
SessionLocal = sessionmaker(bind=engine)

store = SQLAlchemyUserStore(SessionLocal)
store.metadata.create_all(engine)

email_sender = SMTPEmailSender(
    host=SMTP_HOST,
    port=SMTP_PORT,
    username=SMTP_USERNAME,
    password=SMTP_PASSWORD,
    from_email=SMTP_FROM_EMAIL,
    template_dir=Path(__file__).parent.parent / "email_templates",
    template_context={
        "app_url": APP_URL,
    },
)

harbor = UserHarbor(
    secret_key=SECRET_KEY,
    store=store,
    email_sender=email_sender,
)

The custom email directory can override individual templates. Add these two files so verification and recovery messages point to our routes. Other account notifications use the SMTP adapter's default templates.

app/email_templates/verification.html
<p>Hello {{ username }},</p>
<p>
  <a href="{{ app_url.rstrip('/') }}/auth/verify_email?token={{ token | urlencode }}">Activate your account</a>
</p>
app/email_templates/password_reset.html
<p>Hello {{ username }},</p>
<p>
  <a href="{{ app_url.rstrip('/') }}/auth/reset_password?token={{ token | urlencode }}">Reset your password</a>
</p>

Define the return type used by routes. A route can return HTML, a response, or HTML together with HTMX response headers. UserLike describes the public user fields; it does not expose the password hash.

app/core/types.py
from fasthtml.common import FT, HttpHeader, Response
from userharbor.interfaces import UserLike

type HTMLResult = FT | Response | tuple[FT | HttpHeader, ...]
User = UserLike

items.title: HTML document, assets, and loading indicator
items.text:
Every page uses BaseLayout. It loads HTMX, Basecoat's JavaScript, and the stylesheet generated from Basecoat's nova theme. The Tailwind development integration builds the CSS and watches for class changes while the app runs.

hx_boost="true" lets ordinary internal links navigate through HTMX. They still have real URLs, including pagination query parameters. A boosted link normally replaces the body contents and updates browser history.

The single Spinner has htmx-indicator, which hides it while idle. hx_indicator is inherited from the body, so forms and links use this indicator without repeating its selector. The #alerts container receives feedback from any form.

app/layouts/base.py
from fasthtml.common import (
    FT,
    Body,
    Div,
    Head,
    Html,
    Meta,
    Script,
    Title,
)
from fasthtml_basecoat import (
    BasecoatInput,
    BasecoatJS,
    Spinner,
)
from fasthtml_tailwindcss import TailwindHead


def BaseLayout(*c, title: str, **kwargs) -> FT:
    return Html(
        Head(
            Title(title),
            Meta(charset="utf-8"),
            Meta(name="viewport", content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1"),
            Script(src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/htmx.org@2.0.11/dist/htmx.js"),
            BasecoatJS(),
            TailwindHead(input=BasecoatInput("nova"), watch=True),
        ),
        Body(
            Spinner(
                id="global-spinner",
                cls="fixed left-1/2 top-1/2 -translate-x-1/2 -translate-y-1/2 z-50 pointer-events-none size-10 htmx-indicator",
            ),
            Div(
                id="alerts",
                cls="fixed top-4 inset-x-0 z-50 flex flex-col items-center gap-4",
            ),
            *c,
            hx_boost="true",
            hx_indicator="#global-spinner",
        ),
        **kwargs,
    )

items.title: Authentication and dashboard shells
items.text:
The authentication layout adds a theme switcher. Cards will handle the actual forms and messages.

app/layouts/auth.py
from fasthtml.common import (
    FT,
    Div,
)
from fasthtml_basecoat import (
    ThemeSwitcher,
)

from .base import BaseLayout


def AuthLayout(*c, title: str, **kwargs) -> FT:
    return BaseLayout(
        Div(
            ThemeSwitcher(),
            cls="fixed top-4 right-4 z-50 flex items-center gap-4",
        ),
        *c,
        title=title,
        **kwargs,
    )

For the dashboard, keep a small header containing the current user's profile link and a logout button. This tutorial uses a compact shell; the starter adds a responsive sidebar and a fuller navigation bar.

app/layouts/dashboard.py
from urllib.parse import quote

from core.types import User
from fasthtml.common import FT, A, Div, Header, Main, Span
from fasthtml_basecoat import Button, ThemeSwitcher

from .base import BaseLayout


def DashboardLayout(*c, title: str, user: User) -> FT:
    return BaseLayout(
        Header(
            A("Users", href="/"),
            Span(title),
            A(user.username, href=f"/users/{quote(user.username, safe='')}"),
            Button(
                "Logout",
                type="button",
                variant="ghost",
                hx_post="/auth/logout",

items.title: Return form feedback as HTML
items.text:
Create a shared Alert component. The outer element uses hx_swap_oob="beforeend:#alerts", so HTMX appends the returned message to the layout's alert container even when a form uses hx_swap="none".

Domain errors can therefore be displayed without replacing the form or erasing the user's input. UserHarborError remains a domain exception; rendering the message is the application's responsibility.

app/components/alert.py
from typing import Literal

from fasthtml.common import FT, H2, Div, Footer, Section
from fasthtml_basecoat import Button
from fasthtml_lucide import Icon


def Alert(heading: str, message: str, variant: Literal["info", "error"]) -> FT:
    return Div(
        Div(
            Icon("info"),
            H2(heading),
            Section(message),
            Footer(
                Button(
                    Icon("circle-x"),
                    aria_label="Close",
                    data_tooltip="Close",
                    data_side="bottom",
                    data_variant="ghost",
                    onclick="this.closest('.alert').remove()",
                ),
            ),
            cls="alert w-full max-w-md",
            data_variant="destructive" if variant == "error" else None,
            hx_on__load="setTimeout(() => { this.remove() }, 10000)",
        ),
        hx_swap_oob="beforeend:#alerts",
    )

items.title: Login
items.text:

items.title: Connect authentication forms to UserHarbor
items.text:
Create app/routes/auth.py. This is a mounted FastHTML application: its local /login route will be available at /auth/login after we mount it.

Start with the imports, router, and page route:

app/routes/auth.py
from components.alert import Alert
from components.auth.forgot_password import SuccessfulForgotPasswordCard

from components.auth.reset_password import SuccessfulResetPasswordCard
from core.harbor import harbor

from fasthtml.common import FT, HttpHeader, Response, fast_app
from pages.auth import AuthPage
from pages.reset_password import ResetPasswordPage
from pages.verify_email import VerifyEmailPage
from userharbor.exceptions import UserHarborError

@rt(methods=["GET"])

items.title: Register and verify an account
items.text:
Append these handlers to app/routes/auth.py. Registration calls harbor.register(), which validates the account, hashes the password, stores the verification token hash, and sends the verification email.

The email link opens a GET route with token in the query string. Successful verification activates the account so the user can log in. The page avoids sending the token URL as a referrer and is not cached.

app/routes/auth.py
@rt(methods=["POST"])
def register(username: str, email: str, password: str) -> HTMLResult:
    try:
        harbor.register(username, email, password)
    except UserHarborError as e:
        return Alert("Registration Failed", str(e), variant="error")
    return SuccessfulRegisterCard()


@rt(methods=["GET"])
def verify_email(token: str) -> HTMLResult:
    try:
        harbor.verify_email(token)
    except UserHarborError as e:
        page = VerifyEmailPage(error=str(e))
    else:
        page = VerifyEmailPage()
    return (
        page,
        HttpHeader("Referrer-Policy", "no-referrer"),
        HttpHeader("Cache-Control", "no-store"),
    )

items.title: Log in with an HttpOnly session cookie
items.text:
Append the login handler. harbor.login() returns the raw session token; UserHarbor persists its hash. The web application stores the raw token in an HttpOnly cookie, so page scripts do not need to read it.

A successful HTMX login returns HTTP 200 with HX-Redirect, which makes the browser load /. Do not combine this header with a 3xx response: HTMX does not process response headers on 3xx responses.

secure=False is for local HTTP development. Set it to True when deploying behind HTTPS.

app/routes/auth.py
@rt(methods=["POST"])
def login(username: str, password: str) -> HTMLResult:
    try:
        session_token = harbor.login(username, password)
    except UserHarborError as e:
        return Alert("Login Failed", str(e), variant="error")
    response = Response(headers={"HX-Redirect": "/"})
    response.set_cookie(
        "session_token",
        session_token,
        path="/",
        httponly=True,
        secure=False,  # Set to True in production with HTTPS
        samesite="lax",
    )
    return response

items.title: Log out
items.text:
Logout should invalidate the server-side session as well as clear the cookie. An already expired session can be treated as logged out. Append:

app/routes/auth.py
@rt(methods=["POST"])
def logout(request) -> HTMLResult:
    try:
        harbor.logout(request.cookies.get("session_token", ""))
    except UserHarborError:
        pass
    response = Response(headers={"HX-Redirect": "/auth/"})
    response.delete_cookie("session_token", path="/")
    return response

items.title: Recover a forgotten password
items.text:
Append the recovery handlers. harbor.send_password_reset() sends a token when the address is known and returns neutrally for unknown addresses. The email link opens ResetPasswordPage; its form submits the token and new password.

harbor.reset_password() validates the token and password, changes the password, and invalidates all sessions for that user. The success card sends the user back to login.

app/routes/auth.py
@rt(methods=["POST"])
def forgot_password(email: str) -> HTMLResult:
    try:
        harbor.send_password_reset(email)
    except UserHarborError as e:
        return Alert("Password Reset Failed", str(e), variant="error")
    return SuccessfulForgotPasswordCard()


@rt(methods=["GET"])
def reset_password(token: str) -> HTMLResult:
    return (
        ResetPasswordPage(token),
        HttpHeader("Referrer-Policy", "no-referrer"),
        HttpHeader("Cache-Control", "no-store"),
    )


@rt(methods=["POST"])
def update_password(token: str, new_password: str, confirm_password: str) -> HTMLResult:
    if new_password != confirm_password:
        return Alert(
            "Password Reset Failed", "Passwords do not match.", variant="error"
        )
    try:
        harbor.reset_password(new_password=new_password, reset_token=token)
    except UserHarborError as e:
        return Alert("Password Reset Failed", str(e), variant="error")
    return SuccessfulResetPasswordCard()

items.title: List users with query-string pagination
items.text:
Create the table component. Profile links contain URL-encoded usernames; HTML text is escaped by FastHTML.

app/components/user_table.py
from urllib.parse import quote

from fasthtml.common import FT, A, Tbody, Td, Th, Thead, Tr
from fasthtml_basecoat import Table
from userharbor.interfaces import UserList


def UserTable(users: UserList) -> FT:
    return Table(
        Thead(
            Tr(
                Th("Username"),
                Th("Email"),
                Th("Verified"),
            )
        ),
        Tbody(
            *[
                Tr(
                    Td(
                        A(
                            u.username,
                            href=f"/users/{quote(u.username, safe='')}",
                            cls="hover:underline",
                        )
                    ),
                    Td(u.email),
                    Td("Yes" if u.verified else "No"),
                )
                for u in users.items
            ]
        ),
    )

Use the installed Basecoat Pagination and PaginationLink wrappers. Links such as ?page=2 work as normal URLs and inherit boosted navigation from the body. The active page gets aria-current="page" from PaginationLink(current=True).

app/components/pagination.py
from fasthtml.common import FT
from fasthtml_basecoat import Pagination as BasePagination
from fasthtml_basecoat import PaginationLink


def Pagination(page: int, total_pages: int) -> FT | None:
    return (
        BasePagination(
            PaginationLink("Previous", href=f"?page={page - 1}") if page > 1 else None,
            *(
                PaginationLink(
                    str(number), href=f"?page={number}", current=number == page
                )
                for number in range(1, total_pages + 1)
            ),
            PaginationLink("Next", href=f"?page={page + 1}")
            if page < total_pages
            else None,
        )
        if total_pages > 1
        else None
    )

Compose them into a page using DashboardLayout. The user argument is the signed-in viewer, used by the header.

from core.types import User
from fasthtml.common import FT
from layouts.dashboard import DashboardLayout
from userharbor.interfaces import UserList


def UsersPage(users: UserList, user: User, page: int, total_pages: int) -> FT:
    return DashboardLayout(
        UserTable(users),
        Pagination(page, total_pages),
        title="Users",
        user=user,
    )

Create the users router. FastHTML parses page: int = 1 from the query string. harbor.users.list() accepts limit and offset, and returns both the items and the total number of matching users. That total determines the page count.

Clamp page numbers to the available range. An empty database still renders the first page with an empty table. The details handler will be added in the next step.

app/routes/users.py
from core.harbor import harbor
from core.types import HTMLResult
from fasthtml.common import HTTPException, fast_app
from pages.user_details import UserDetailsPage
from pages.users import UsersPage

users_app, rt = fast_app()


@rt(methods=["GET"])
def index(request, page: int = 1) -> HTMLResult:
    page_size = 10
    page = max(1, page)
    users = harbor.users.list(limit=page_size, offset=(page - 1) * page_size)
    total_pages = max(1, (users.total + page_size - 1) // page_size)
    if page > total_pages:
        page = total_pages
        users = harbor.users.list(limit=page_size, offset=(page - 1) * page_size)
    return UsersPage(users, request.scope.get("user"), page, total_pages)

See User Manager for searching and sorting as well.

@rt("/users/{username}", methods=["GET"])

    if profile is None:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail="User not found")
    return UserDetailsPage(profile, request.scope["user"])

items.title: Change passwords and delete the signed-in account
items.text:
Create a separate mounted router at /account. These operations take their identity from the session cookie, not from a submitted username or the profile URL. UserHarbor validates the token and current password before changing the account.

On a successful password change, all sessions are invalidated. Both successful operations clear the browser cookie and redirect to login. Errors return the same out-of-band alert used by the authentication forms.

The deletion handler also checks confirmed on the server. Hiding a form or disabling a button alone is not authorization.

app/routes/account.py
from components.alert import Alert
from core.harbor import harbor
from core.types import HTMLResult
from fasthtml.common import Response, fast_app
from userharbor.exceptions import UserHarborError

account_app, rt = fast_app()


@rt(methods=["POST"])
def change_password(
    request, old_password: str, new_password: str, confirm_password: str
) -> HTMLResult:
    if new_password != confirm_password:
        return Alert(
            "Password Change Failed", "Passwords do not match.", variant="error"
        )
    try:
        harbor.change_password(
            old_password=old_password,
            new_password=new_password,
            session_token=request.cookies.get("session_token", ""),
        )
    except UserHarborError as e:
        return Alert("Password Change Failed", str(e), variant="error")
    response = Response(headers={"HX-Redirect": "/auth/"})
    response.delete_cookie("session_token", path="/")
    return response


@rt(methods=["POST"])
def delete(request, password: str, confirmed: bool = False) -> HTMLResult:
    if not confirmed:
        return Alert(
            "Account Deletion Failed",
            "Confirm account deletion first.",
            variant="error",
        )
    try:
        harbor.delete_account(
            password=password,
            session_token=request.cookies.get("session_token", ""),
        )
    except UserHarborError as e:
        return Alert("Account Deletion Failed", str(e), variant="error")
    response = Response(headers={"HX-Redirect": "/auth/"})
    response.delete_cookie("session_token", path="/")
    return response

items.title: Protect pages and mount the routers
items.text:
Create app/main.py. The root middleware validates the session before dispatching to any mounted application and puts the current user in request.scope["user"]. A hook on just one child FastHTML application would not protect its siblings.

Authentication pages and static assets remain accessible without a session. Authenticated users are sent away from the login screen, while logout and email verification/recovery links remain available.

Ordinary requests use a 303 redirect. For HTMX requests, the middleware returns HX-Redirect with HTTP 200 so an expired session navigates to the login page instead of inserting it into an existing form or alert target.

app/main.py
from contextlib import suppress

from core.harbor import harbor
from fasthtml.common import FastHTML, Response, StaticImmutable
from routes.account import account_app
from routes.auth import auth_app
from routes.users import users_app
from starlette.middleware import Middleware
from starlette.middleware.base import BaseHTTPMiddleware
from starlette.responses import RedirectResponse
from starlette.routing import Mount
from userharbor.exceptions import UserHarborError


def redirect(request, url: str):
    if request.headers.get("HX-Request") == "true":
        return Response(headers={"HX-Redirect": url})
    return RedirectResponse(url, status_code=303)


async def check_session(request, call_next):
    path = request.url.path
    user = None
    if token := request.cookies.get("session_token"):
        with suppress(UserHarborError):
            user = harbor.get_current_user(token)
    request.scope["user"] = user

    public = path == "/auth" or path.startswith(("/auth/", "/static/"))
    if user and path in ("/auth", "/auth/", "/auth/login", "/auth/register"):
        return redirect(request, "/")
    if not user and not public:
        response = redirect(request, "/auth/")
        response.delete_cookie("session_token", path="/")
        return response
    return await call_next(request)


app = FastHTML(
    middleware=[Middleware(BaseHTTPMiddleware, dispatch=check_session)],
    routes=[
        Mount("/static", StaticImmutable(directory="static"), name="static"),
        Mount("/auth", auth_app, name="auth"),
        Mount("/account", account_app, name="account"),
        Mount("/", users_app, name="index"),
    ],
)

items.title: Run the application
items.text:
From the project root, start the application with the environment file:

cd app
uv run --env-file ../.env uvicorn main:app --reload

Open http://localhost:8000. Running from app/ also makes the core, routes, pages, and components imports resolve and places users.db beside main.py.

Try the complete flow:

  1. Register an account and follow the verification link sent by email.
  2. Log in and open your profile from the header or user table.
  3. Create enough accounts to navigate to ?page=2 and back.
  4. View another user's profile: the password and deletion forms are absent.
  5. Change your password and log in again with the new one.
  6. Log out, request a reset email, and set a new password through its link.
  7. On your own profile, confirm deletion and enter your password to remove the account.

While a request is running, the shared spinner appears and that form's controls are disabled. If a domain operation fails, an alert appears without replacing the form. The logout button disables only itself.

items.title: How the HTMX pieces fit together
items.text:
Attribute or header Purpose in this application hx-boost Navigate internal links through HTML requests and update browser history. hx-post Submit form values to a FastHTML route. hx-swap="none" Leave the form in place unless the response explicitly replaces it. hx-swap-oob Append feedback to the shared alerts container. HX-Retarget and HX-Reswap Replace a card after a successful operation. HX-Redirect Navigate to a new page after login, logout, or account changes. hx-disabled-elt Disable selected form controls or the triggering button during a request. hx-indicator Show the shared loading indicator during a request.

These attributes describe browser behavior directly beside the UI that triggers it. The routes keep returning HTML; UserHarbor remains independent of HTMX and FastHTML. See the HTMX documentation for boosted navigation, disabled controls, and redirect responses.

items.title: Continue with the starter
items.text:
The FastHTML Starter repository contains the complete application shown in the presentation, including the responsive dashboard sidebar and navigation components. Its structure follows the same settings → components → layouts → pages → routes separation used here.

Before deploying your own application, configure HTTPS and secure cookies, protect cookie-authenticated state-changing routes against CSRF, keep secrets outside version control, and decide who may view the user directory. Use your normal deployment process for database migrations, SMTP delivery, and rate limits.

For a deeper explanation of this architecture, read Hypermedia Systems, the free book from the creators of HTMX.
